doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Closing and Stravinsky's creative process
summary: Closing thanks with remarks about motifs, Ravel on the Rite of Spring and Stravinsky's Poetics of Music.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: Okay. Well this has really been fascinating.
I appreciate it. Thanks for your time. I hope those germs keep coming.
Oh they will. The guy on the radio, he thought I meant real germs. I said no, no, I’m talking about motifs. Motifs.
Right. Like a computer virus, like uh oh.

But I can tell the difference between just a b.s. one and one that’s coming from that special place that’s loaded with that spiritual energy. So that’s a real germ. He said, “Yeah, there’s a piece of music within that.” Stravinsky and Ravel had a lot of admiration for each other. And so Ravel made this statement about Stravinsky once. He said, “The miracle of the ‘Rite of Spring’ lies in its entity.” So I had a lot of students say, “What does he mean by that?” So I said, “I think he means that look how [scats] became ‘The Rite of Spring?” He went from that and then that just kept developing and it becomes a whole big — so that’s the way he composed. There’s a book, I don’t know if you ever read it, The Poetics of Music by Stravinsky. It’s six lectures, I think it was at Yale or Harvard. It’s a very enlightening book. He talks about the way he creates music, his creative process. And I remember learning a lot from that book about what we’re talking about.
Cool. I’ll have to get that. I love that music. Okay. Thank you.
